Almost every AWS security service depends on KMS: S3 EBS RDS Secrets Manager EKS Lambda CloudWatch Logs SNS SQS Understanding KMS is essential for designing secure AWS architectures. In a multi-account setup under AWS Organizations, resources are spread across many member accounts. Logging in to each account to check what is running takes a lot of time. AWS Config solves this. From the management account, you can query resources in all member accounts in one place: Running EC2 instances S3 bucket details VPC details Any other resource that Config records

AWS Organization └── Account A → Management account (we run queries from here) ├── Account B → Member ├── Account C → Member └── Account D → Member Requirement: list the running EC2 instances in accounts B and C, without logging in to them.

AWS Config recording is enabled in the member accounts and Regions you want to query. This is usually rolled out with CloudFormation StackSets or Control Tower. An organization aggregator exists in the management account (or a delegated admin account): AWS Config → Aggregators → Create aggregator → Add my organization. This aggregator is what collects data from all member accounts.
AWS Config → Advanced queries → New query
In Query scope, select the organization aggregator, not "This account only". This is the key step. Without it, the query only sees the management account's own resources.
documents.s: 3. Set the query scope to the organization

documents.t: Running EC2 instances in accounts B and C: SELECT accountId, awsRegion, resourceId, configuration.instanceType, configuration.state.name WHERE resourceType = 'AWS::EC2::Instance' AND configuration.state.name = 'running' AND accountId IN ('222222222222', '333333333333') -- Account B, Account C Remove the accountId line to see running instances across all member accounts.

All S3 buckets across the organization: SELECT accountId, awsRegion, resourceName, resourceCreationTime WHERE resourceType = 'AWS::S3::Bucket' All VPCs with their CIDR ranges: SELECT accountId, awsRegion, resourceId, configuration.cidrBlock WHERE resourceType = 'AWS::EC2::VPC' Same query from the CLI: aws configservice select-aggregate-resource-config \ --configuration-aggregator-name org-aggregator \ --expression "SELECT accountId, resourceId WHERE resourceType = 'AWS::EC2::Instance' AND configuration.state.name = 'running'"

tip Results are only as complete as the recording. If Config isn't enabled in a member account or Region, that account's or Region's resources won't appear. Data comes from Config's recorded snapshot, so it can lag a few minutes behind live state. Save frequently used queries in Advanced queries so the team can re-run them.

To use an AWS Local Zone, first you need to enable / opt in to the Local Zone from the AWS console or CLI. For Local Zone networking, you do not need to create a new VPC. A VPC can span Availability Zones and Local Zones. You only need to create a new subnet inside the existing VPC and select the enabled Local Zone as the subnet location. ([AWS Documentation][1])
Enable Local Zone ↓ Select existing VPC ↓ Create subnet in Local Zone ↓ Launch supported resources in that Local Zone subnet

To use an AWS Local Zone, we must first opt in to the Local Zone. After enabling it, we do not need to create a new VPC. We can extend an existing VPC by creating a subnet in the Local Zone and then launch supported resources in that subnet.

This page explains with pictures how to look at a VPC and understand it: which subnet is public, which is private, and whether a server can reach the internet. Colour guide used in every diagram: 🟩 Green = public · 🟦 Blue = private app · 🟧 Orange = database · ⬜ Grey = internet / AWS gateways

When you create a subnet, AWS never asks "public or private?". The name public-subnet-1a is only a label. 👉 If the subnet's route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an Internet Gateway, it's public. Otherwise it's private. How to check in the console: VPC → Subnets → select the subnet → Route table tab → look at where 0.0.0.0/0 goes. info "Auto-assign public IPv4 address" does not make a subnet public. It only gives new instances a public IP. Without the route to the IGW, that IP is useless.

documents.t: Think of it like sending a letter: you need a road out (IGW route) and a return address (public IP). Without either one, the reply never comes back. Reachable from internet? 1 Public Yes ✅ Yes ✅ Yes (if the security group allows it) 2 Public No ❌ No ❌ No 3 Private + NAT No ✅ Yes, through NAT ❌ No 4 Private, no NAT No ❌ No ❌ No

documents.t: No. It has the road (IGW route) but no return address (public IP), so yum update or curl google.com simply times out. A NAT route can't help either, because that route table's 0.0.0.0/0 already points to the IGW.

documents.t: Some banking projects put EC2 instances in public subnets but disable public IPs for compliance, and put a load balancer in front of them. Reading the picture: ✅ Users reach the ALB, which has public IPs. ✅ The ALB forwards traffic to the EC2 instances' private IPs, so users can use the app. ❌ The EC2 instances can't go out to the internet (no public IP). ✅ They can still reach AWS services privately through VPC endpoints: a Gateway endpoint for S3/DynamoDB, Interface endpoints for SSM, ECR and Secrets Manager. tip If those servers need outbound internet, the cleaner design is the one in Lesson 4: move them to private subnets with a NAT Gateway.
documents.s: Lesson 3: Banking scenario, public subnet with no public IPs

documents.t: Student question: "Can I keep all EC2 instances and databases private and expose only the ALB?" Yes. This is the recommended AWS three-tier design. Question Answer Is a public subnet mandatory? Yes, for an internet-facing ALB Must EC2 instances be in public subnets? No Can the ALB forward to private EC2 instances? Yes, using their private IPs Can an internet-facing ALB use only private subnets? No Can the database stay fully private? Yes, and it should Remember: An ALB needs at least two subnets in different AZs. There are two kinds of ALB: an internet-facing ALB goes in public subnets; an internal ALB goes in private subnets and is reachable only from inside the network. The ALB only handles incoming traffic. Private servers still need a NAT Gateway or VPC endpoints to go out. Add AWS WAF on the ALB for extra protection.
documents.s: Lesson 4: Recommended design, only the ALB is public

documents.t: Two of everything, one in each AZ, so losing one AZ doesn't take the application down. Subnet Route 0.0.0.0/0 goes to What lives here 🟩 Public Internet Gateway ALB, NAT Gateway 🟦 Private app NAT Gateway (in the same AZ) EC2, EKS nodes 🟧 Private DB Nowhere (no internet route) RDS tip Use one NAT Gateway per AZ in production. With only one, if that AZ fails, every private server loses outbound internet.

documents.t: Teams moving from Classic (UI-based) pipelines to YAML often hit the same problems: They don't know where the YAML file must live or how Azure DevOps finds it. They mix up stages, jobs and steps, so builds and deployments run in the wrong order. A file built in one job is "missing" in the next job, because each job on a Microsoft-hosted agent runs on a brand-new VM. Deployments run when they shouldn't (for example, a feature branch deploying to production) because conditions are missing or wrong. This page explains how a pipeline is structured, how files and values move through it, and the setup that is recommended for production.

Term Meaning Pipeline The whole YAML definition: triggers, variables, stages. One run = one execution. Stage A logical boundary (Build, Test, Deploy-Dev, Deploy-Prod). Stages run one after another by default. Job A unit of work that runs on one agent. Jobs in a stage run in parallel by default. Deployment job A special job (deployment:) that targets an environment, records deployment history and supports approvals and strategies (runOnce, rolling, canary). Step One action in a job: a task, script, bash, pwsh, checkout, publish, download or template. Steps run sequentially. Task A packaged, reusable step, for example DotNetCoreCLI@2 or AzureWebApp@1. Agent The machine that runs a job: Microsoft-hosted or self-hosted. Agent pool A group of agents. A job asks for a pool; any free agent in it picks up the job. Pipeline artifact Files published from one job and downloaded in later jobs/stages of the same run (or other pipelines). Environment A deployment target (dev, prod) with approvals, checks and history.

When you create a pipeline with the wizard (Pipelines → New pipeline → choose repo → Starter pipeline), Azure DevOps creates: <repo-root>/azure-pipelines.yml info The default name is azure-pipelines.yml (plural "pipelines", no leading dot). It is only a convention. Any file name, any folder, and either .yml or .yaml works.

Point the pipeline to any path when you create it: Pipelines → New pipeline, then select the repository. Choose Existing Azure Pipelines YAML file. Select the branch and path, for example /.azure-pipelines/ci.yml. For an existing pipeline: Edit → ⋮ (more actions) → Triggers → YAML tab → YAML file path. With the Azure CLI: create-pipeline.sh # Requires the azure-devops CLI extension: az extension add --name azure-devops az pipelines create \ --name "app-ci-cd" \ --repository "my-app" \ --repository-type tfsgit \ --branch main \ --yml-path ".azure-pipelines/ci-cd.yml" # custom path instead of the root default

my-app/ ├── src/ ├── .azure-pipelines/ │ ├── ci-cd.yml # main pipeline (entry point) │ ├── pr-validation.yml # optional separate PR pipeline │ └── templates/ │ ├── build-job.yml # reusable job template │ ├── deploy-stage.yml # reusable stage template (dev/prod) │ └── variables-common.yml # shared variables └── README.md tip Keep pipelines in a dedicated folder and move repeated logic into templates. One deploy-stage.yml template used for dev, test and prod ensures every environment is deployed the same way.

Pipeline (trigger, pr, variables, pool, resources, parameters) └── stages ├── stage: Build │ └── jobs │ ├── job: Compile ← runs on agent #1 │ │ └── steps: checkout → script → publish │ └── job: UnitTest ← runs on agent #2 (parallel by default) │ └── steps: ... └── stage: Deploy ← waits for Build by default └── jobs └── deployment: DeployWeb ← targets environment 'prod' └── strategy → runOnce → deploy → steps Rules: A pipeline has one or more stages. Stages run sequentially (each one depends on the one before it) unless you set dependsOn. A stage has one or more jobs. Jobs run in parallel unless you set dependsOn, and only if you have enough parallel-job capacity. A job has one or more steps, which always run sequentially on the same agent.

You don't always have to write every level. Azure DevOps fills in the missing levels for you: 1-steps-only.yml # Single stage + single job: write steps directly. # Azure DevOps creates an implicit stage and an implicit job named "Job". trigger: [main] pool: vmImage: ubuntu-latest steps: - script: echo "Hello from the implicit job" displayName: Say hello 2-jobs-only.yml # Single stage, multiple jobs: write jobs directly (implicit stage). trigger: [main] jobs: - job: Build pool: vmImage: ubuntu-latest steps: - script: echo "build" - job: Lint pool: vmImage: ubuntu-latest steps: - script: echo "lint" # runs in parallel with Build 3-full-stages.yml # Multiple stages: full hierarchy. trigger: [main] stages: - stage: Build jobs: - job: Compile pool: vmImage: ubuntu-latest steps: - script: echo "compile" - stage: Deploy # runs after Build (implicit dependsOn: Build) jobs: - job: Release pool: vmImage: ubuntu-latest steps: - script: echo "deploy" You write at the top level Azure DevOps creates Use when steps: 1 implicit stage + 1 implicit job Simple CI: build/test in one place jobs: 1 implicit stage CI with parallel jobs (build, lint, tests on different OSes) stages: Nothing implicit CI + CD, approvals, multiple environments (production) warning You can't mix these levels at the top. If you write stages:, you can't also write jobs: or steps: at the root of the file.

CopyFiles@2 only copies files on the same agent, usually into $(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory) to prepare a clean package. To move files to another job or stage, you need pipeline artifacts. Job A (agent #1) Job B (agent #2) build → CopyFiles → staging dir → publish ───► Azure DevOps ───► download → $(Pipeline.Workspace)/drop artifact storage

documents.t: Same stage, Job A → Job B​ same-stage-artifact.yml jobs: - job: Build pool: vmImage: ubuntu-latest steps: - script: | mkdir -p dist echo "app v1" > dist/app.txt displayName: Build app - task: CopyFiles@2 # stage only what you want to ship inputs: SourceFolder: dist Contents: '**' TargetFolder: $(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory) - publish: $(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory) artifact: drop # artifact name displayName: Publish artifact 'drop' - job: Test dependsOn: Build # REQUIRED: otherwise runs in parallel and the artifact isn't there yet pool: vmImage: ubuntu-latest steps: - download: current # 'current' = this pipeline run artifact: drop - script: cat $(Pipeline.Workspace)/drop/app.txt displayName: Use the file Different stage, Build stage → Deploy stage​ cross-stage-artifact.yml stages: - stage: Build jobs: - job: Build pool: vmImage: ubuntu-latest steps: - script: echo "app v1" > $(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory)/app.txt - publish: $(Build.ArtifactStagingDirectory) artifact: drop - stage: Deploy dependsOn: Build jobs: # Normal job: you must download explicitly - job: Verify pool: vmImage: ubuntu-latest steps: - download: current artifact: drop - script: ls -R $(Pipeline.Workspace)/drop # Deployment job: artifacts of the current run are downloaded AUTOMATICALLY - deployment: DeployWeb environment: dev pool: vmImage: ubuntu-latest strategy: runOnce: deploy: steps: - script: ls -R $(Pipeline.Workspace)/drop # already there info Artifacts belong to the run, so any later job or stage in the same run can download them. The download location is $(Pipeline.Workspace)/<artifact-name>. In a deployment job, add - download: none if you don't want the automatic download (it saves time). PublishBuildArtifacts@1 / DownloadBuildArtifacts@0 (build artifacts) are the older approach. Prefer pipeline artifacts, which are faster and deduplicated. Between different pipelines (CI pipeline → CD pipeline)​ cd-pipeline.yml resources: pipelines: - pipeline: ci # alias used below source: app-ci # name of the CI pipeline in Azure DevOps trigger: branches: [main] # run CD automatically when CI on main succeeds steps: - download: ci # download artifacts from the CI run that triggered this artifact: drop

Push outputs to an external store and pull them later: Store Good for Azure Container Registry Container images (build once, promote the same image through every environment) Azure Artifacts feeds (Universal Packages, npm, NuGet, Maven) Versioned packages shared across pipelines and teams Azure Storage (Blob) Very large files, or files that must outlive pipeline retention

Pipeline artifacts External storage Setup None, built in Service connection, RBAC, storage Scope Same run / linked pipelines Anything, any system Retention Follows the run's retention policy You control it Security Azure DevOps permissions Azure RBAC / private endpoints Best for Build output → test → deploy Images, shared packages, long-lived files

Application packages (zip, jar, static sites): pipeline artifacts. Build once in the Build stage and deploy the same artifact to dev → test → prod. Never rebuild per environment, so what you tested is exactly what you ship. Container images: push to ACR in the Build stage, tagged with $(Build.BuildId) or the git SHA, and pass only the tag to later stages (see the next section). Don't rely on shared folders on self-hosted agents. Jobs can land on different agents, and parallel runs overwrite each other.

Viewpoint What this design gives you Architect Build once, promote many: the tested artifact is exactly what reaches prod. Separate service connections per environment limit how far a mistake can reach. Approvals live on the environment, not in YAML, so they can't be removed by editing the file. Implementation engineer Stages = environments, jobs = units of work, artifacts = hand-over between them. Templates remove repetition when more environments are added. L2 / operations Environment history shows which run and commit is deployed where. Rollback = re-run the Prod stage of the last good run. Failed stage logs show the exact step.

tip Use stages: for anything that deploys. Keep steps:-only pipelines for simple CI. Build once, publish once, and deploy the same artifact everywhere. Always add dependsOn when a job needs another job's output. Use deployment jobs + environments for deployments, which give you approvals, history and auto-download. Use service connections with workload identity federation (no secrets to rotate). Keep secrets in variable groups linked to Azure Key Vault, never in YAML. Use templates for repeated stages and jobs, and pin template repos with ref:. Wrap custom conditions in and(succeeded(), ...). Pin images/versions you depend on (for example ubuntu-24.04 instead of ubuntu-latest) when reproducibility matters more than staying current.

Q1. What's the difference between a stage, a job and a step? A stage is a logical phase (Build, Deploy) and stages run sequentially by default. A job runs on one agent, and jobs inside a stage run in parallel by default. A step is a single task or script, and steps run sequentially inside a job. Q2. Can you write a pipeline without stages or jobs? Yes. With only steps:, Azure DevOps creates an implicit stage and job. With only jobs:, it creates an implicit stage. Q3. How do you pass a build output from one stage to another? publish it as a pipeline artifact in the build job and download: current it in the later job. Deployment jobs download the current run's artifacts automatically. Q4. Why is a file missing in the second job on a Microsoft-hosted agent? Every job gets a fresh VM that is discarded afterwards. Files must be passed through artifacts. Q5. When would you choose self-hosted agents? When jobs need private network access (private endpoints, on-premises), custom or licensed tools, large persistent caches, or compliance control over the build machine.

These variables exist by default within GitLab and provide information about the project, pipeline, or commit. Examples include: CI_COMMIT_BRANCH: Shows the branch where changes were committed. CI_PROJECT_NAME: The name of the project. CI_PIPELINE_ID: A unique ID for every pipeline run.

These are variables created by the user to store specific values needed for the pipeline, such as database usernames or environment names. They are typically created in the GitLab project settings under Settings > CI/CD > Variables.

Secrets are a specific category of custom variables used for sensitive data, such as passwords, API keys, tokens, and SSH keys. The video emphasizes a critical rule: never hardcode secrets directly into the pipeline script or source code to avoid leaking them in logs or to unauthorized users.

Masking is a security feature applied to variables so their values do not appear in the pipeline logs. When a variable is masked, GitLab replaces the value with stars (e.g., **********) in the logs. To be masked, a value must be at least eight characters long and contain no spaces.

These variables are restricted so they are only available to jobs running on protected branches (like the main branch). If a developer creates a "malicious" branch to try and print secrets, protected variables will not be visible or accessible in that branch.
When a pipeline runs, GitLab internally injects these variables into the job's environment using an export command. This allows scripts to access the values securely during execution.

The video also explains that variables can be defined at different "scopes," and GitLab follows a specific hierarchy (precedence) if the same variable is defined in multiple places: Pipeline level: Highest priority; passed during the pipeline run. Project level: Available to all pipelines within a specific project. Group level: Shared across multiple projects within a group. Predefined level: The default built-in values.

Cloud computing is the practice of using computing resources over the internet — without buying or managing physical hardware. Typical cloud resources include: Servers Storage Networking Databases Applications Instead of purchasing and maintaining physical servers, cloud providers offer resources on-demand. Popular cloud providers: Google Cloud Platform (GCP) Amazon Web Services (AWS) Microsoft Azure

Google Cloud Platform (GCP) is Google's cloud computing platform. For any cloud platform, Compute and VPC are the two most fundamental services. Once you truly understand these two services, you can confidently say you know that cloud.
Before creating a VM in Google Cloud, let's revisit the components of a typical Linux server. A Linux server contains: Operating System CPU RAM Disk / Storage Private IP Address Public IP Address

documents.s: AWS vs Google Cloud Networking Comparison

documents.t: In AWS: VPC is regional Subnets are Availability Zone specific Example: VPC ├── Subnet-A (us-east-1a) └── Subnet-B (us-east-1b)
In Google Cloud: VPC is global Subnets are regional Example: Global VPC └── Subnet (us-central1) ├── VM in us-central1-a ├── VM in us-central1-b └── VM in us-central1-c
In Google Cloud: Subnet belongs to a region VM belongs to a zone Same subnet can be used across multiple zones inside the same region
Internet ↓ Public IP ↓ Firewall Rule ↓ VPC Network ↓ Subnet ↓ Virtual Machine

Install Nginx web server. sudo apt install nginx -y Start Nginx: sudo systemctl start nginx Enable Nginx: sudo systemctl enable nginx
Open browser: http://PUBLIC_IP At this stage, application may still not work because firewall access is blocked.
Google Cloud blocks incoming traffic by default. To allow HTTP traffic: Port 80 must be opened
Navigate to: VPC Network → Firewall Create Rule: Field Value Name allow-http Direction Ingress Targets All instances Source IP 0.0.0.0/0 Protocols TCP:80
Internet ↓ Firewall Rule (Allow TCP 80) ↓ VM Instance ↓ Nginx Application
Open browser again: http://PUBLIC_IP Nginx default page should load successfully.
